articles.full_text:
Israel’s severe heat wave is expected to reach its peak only on Sunday, but temperatures will already be above average to extremely hot on Saturday, particularly inland and in the mountainous regions.
Conditions along the coastal plain will be hot and humid, while heat stress will intensify across the country. The Israel Meteorological Service warned of heavy to extreme heat stress nationwide.
Temperatures are expected to rise further on Sunday, when the heat wave reaches its peak. Winds will strengthen from the afternoon.
A slight drop in temperatures is expected for the first time on Monday, although conditions will remain hotter than usual for the season and heat stress will persist. Tuesday morning is expected to be clear, with a further decline in temperatures as the heat wave begins to break.
Dr. Amir Givati, director of the Israel Meteorological Service, warned Thursday that people should avoid outdoor activity during the hottest hours. “We need to avoid physical activity during the hours of heavy heat,” he told the ynet studio. “There was a similar heat wave last August, and there were quite a few cases of heatstroke. This is a truly extreme heat event.
“People in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area may not fully understand what we are talking about, but in the north it will be very hot and dry during the afternoon.”
Forecast temperatures for Saturday and overnight: Jerusalem 23-34°C (73-93°F), Tel Aviv 25-32°C (77-90°F), Haifa 24-32°C (75-90°F), Safed 24-36°C (75-97°F), Katzrin 23-40°C (73-104°F), Tiberias 25-40°C (77-104°F), Nazareth 25-37°C (77-99°F), Afula 22-38°C (72-100°F), Beit She’an 27-41°C (81-106°F), Lod 24-34°C (75-93°F), Ashdod 25-32°C (77-90°F), Ein Gedi 31-41°C (88-106°F), Beersheba 23-37°C (73-99°F), Mitzpe Ramon 25-37°C (77-99°F) and Eilat 31-39°C (88-102°F)

Kumamoto quake survivors battle intense heat as death toll rises to 36
A man wipes his sweat while sitting at a warehouse, in which his family keeps food, water and some of their belongings, in Hikawa, Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture, on Friday.
| REUTERS
Survivors of a large earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture earlier this week were battling against intense heat Saturday, as the estimated death toll rose to at least 36.
Over 9,000 evacuees marked their first weekend since Tuesday’s magnitude 7.1 temblor shook the region, while water shortages continued.
Some 229 evacuation shelters were set up Saturday morning, housing around 9,228 people. While power has largely been restored throughout the prefecture, many people were still taking refuge in their cars to escape the heat and stay cool.

‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The Odyssey
In Athens’ picturehouses, an interval is always a ‘non-negotiable’ – a chance to buy a beer, nip to the toilet – or pop the question
As the lights rose during a recent screening of The Odyssey at the Arian open-air cinema on the Athens riviera, nervous laughter floated into the breeze. Moments earlier, Odysseus’s men had morphed into pigs during a grotesque feeding frenzy fuelled by drugged cheese and wine. Now, as the Bangles’ Eternal Flame played on the house speakers, no one seemed especially tempted by the concession stand’s hotdogs.
This is presumably the sort of scenario Christopher Nolan hoped to avoid when he decided against an intermission in his nearly three-hour-long adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey. In the epic’s country of origin, however, directors do not get the final word.
“In Greece, the intermission is a must,” said Fotis Georgopoulos, whose family has run Cine Foivos, a movie house in the Athens suburb of Peristeri, for 72 years. “People want to smoke, they want to go to the toilet, they want to discuss the movie. And they don’t want to lose even five minutes of it.”
At Foivos, The Odyssey’s interval came during a more elegant moment, as Odysseus sailed away from Circe’s island. Outside, Gina Alexopoulou, 24, welcomed the chance to tell her boyfriend that Nolan’s Laestrygonians were the work of seven-foot actors rather than CGI. Nearby, brothers Giorgios and Panagiotis Liolias, both in their 30s, were also having a smoke, though they would have preferred to watch the film uninterrupted.
Until recent years, intermissions were standard practice at cinemas in Athens. In the early days, orchestras and theatrical troupes sometimes entertained audiences as projectionists changed reels. By 1960, when the city had at least 350 movie theatres, the intermission had become a social affair.
The tradition faded somewhat as multiplexes arrived in the late 1990s, independent theatres transitioned to digital projection in the 2000s, and Covid regulations briefly prohibited intermissions altogether. Now, customers who prefer the breaks – typically five to 10 minutes – often check for them at the box office or ticketing site.
At the city’s longstanding summer cinemas, it’s a different story. At the halfway point of most any movie shown outdoors, patrons still shoot the proverbial breeze as they queue for cheese pies, homemade sour cherry juice and the ubiquitous Domino’s Pizza.
Intermissions are still deployed, though increasingly less so, in countries including Switzerland, Egypt, and Turkey, and are de rigueur in India, where Bollywood films are scripted with the interval in mind.
In Greece, they are crucial to cinemas’ survival. When Dafni Bechtsi took over Athens’ troubled Alexandra theatre in 2024 (now the Cinobo Patision), a midway break for refreshments was essential to her business model. Greek cinemas receive “no support from the government or anything, and they’re really struggling”, she said. “The revenue you get during the break, from food and drink, even if it might not be so much, is super critical.”
After winter, cinemas like the Cinobo Patision close for the season to make way for the city’s dozens of open-air ones. The interval becomes a chance to enjoy the bamboo-lined, Cyclades-style terrace at Cine Dexameni, or the view of the Acropolis from the rooftop Cine Paris. Seats are sometimes substituted with hammocks, sunbeds, or garden swings.
In one of the world’s most nocturnal cities, a midnight intermission can also be an opportunity to re-evaluate one’s night altogether and determine whether it’s worth watching the rest of a dud rather than joining friends at a concert or late dinner. Maybe it isn’t just a coincidence that the Greeks refer to the intermission as a diáleimma.
However some audience members remain sceptical. At the Electra, a loud grumble of “for fuck’s sake” greeted a bathroom break that shattered the tension of Backrooms. Other cuts are Oscar-worthy. At the open-air cinema abutting the War Museum, where ushers hand out blankets and pillows during the interval, Obsession was interrupted right as the unhinged protagonist urinated on the floor – the perfect cue to use the loo.
Projectionists have varying approaches to inserting restroom respites. Anastasia Kottaki, who works at Trianon, jumped straight to the middle of The Odyssey’s digital file to identify a suitable scene change. At Cine Alsos, a 61-year-old cinema tucked inside a wooded park, staff watched the movie in its entirety to choose the best moment and avoid stepping on any action sequences.
Mid-screening sales account for about 30% of the Alsos’s profits. Yet owner Giannis Chatzidimitriou insists that the social value of the intermission is equally important. A few years ago, he helped a customer pop the question by screening a proposal video during the interlude. The couple received a standing – and leg-stretching – ovation.
More than one marriage has blossomed over popcorn and passatempo, Greece’s beloved salted pumpkin seeds. Vrasidas Karalis, author of A History of Greek Cinema, recalls a friend meeting her future husband while queueing at the snack bar during Bernardo Bertolucci’s 1900. “Their hands touched, and they started talking about the upcoming revolution and the end of capitalist cruelty,” he says.
Karalis, who grew up in the Greater Athens area and now lives in Australia, says he misses the conversations that unfolded with old-timers working the canteen. “Most of them still are real eccentrics with something interesting to suggest about other films.”
Peggy Ringa, an archaeologist turned cinema-owner, counts herself among those enthusiasts. At her open-air cinemas – the Riviera, Vox and Athinaia – intermissions are “non-negotiable”. Longer films even get two of them. But they can still take visitors unaware.
While Béla Tarr’s two-and-a-half-hour-long Werckmeister Harmonies premiered in the country, said Ringa, the director was alarmed by the sight of audience members filing out of the auditorium halfway through. “The Greek distributors had a very difficult time convincing him that this was perfectly normal.”

articles.full_text:
Extreme heat and wildfire smoke can be dangerous for pets, community cats and other animals. Two Rogue Valley organizations say simple precautions can help keep them safe during the hottest days of summer.
Laurie Cuddy, president of Rogue Valley Street Dogs, said pets belonging to people experiencing homelessness face additional challenges because they may have limited access to shade and water. She said animals can quickly develop heat-related illnesses in extreme temperatures.
"People do everything they can to look out for their animals first," Cuddy said. "But not having access to water is a huge issue, because in the extreme heat animals need much more water."
Rogue Valley Street Dogs distributes supplies including cooling collars, paw wax and protective booties to help keep animals safe. Cuddy said flat-faced breeds such as pugs and bulldogs are especially vulnerable to overheating.
Amanda Linnehan, president and executive director of Rogue Community Cat Rescue, said cats are also at risk during periods of extreme heat. She warned that pet carriers left in the sun can heat up rapidly and become dangerous.
"When a cat pants, it's almost you've hit a point where you have an emergency," Linnehan said. "That cat needs to be cooled off immediately."
Linnehan encourages residents caring for outdoor cat colonies to provide shade and frozen water bottles to help animals stay cool.

articles.title: Three killed in landslides across Kerala; IMD issues 'red alert' for heavy rainfall in several districts - Deccan Herald

articles.full_text:
Amid heavy rainfall that triggered floods and landslides across Kerala, three people lost their lives and several others are trapped following separate landslide incidents in Idukki and Kottayam districts on Saturday.

The deceases in Idukki was identified as Sumathi, a resident of the Adoormala area near Kudayathoor. Debris from a landslide struck her house, which has been destroyed, in the early hours of Saturday, the district administration said.

Neighbours could rescue her husband and the couple's son. Both were injured and have been admitted to a hospital in Thodupuzha.

Sumathi's body was recovered after a search operation carried out by personnel of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Fire and Rescue Services, police and revenue officials.

.Woman killed in Idukki landslide as heavy rain triggers floods across central Kerala.

In another incident, a person identified as Prabhakaran Nair died after a landslide hit a house in the Vagamon area of Idukki district.

Officials said that Nair, a native of Vaikom in Kottayam, was sleeping in one of the bedrooms of his relative's house when the landslide happened. His body was recovered after an hours-long search.

In Kottayam, a youth, identified as Joseph, died, while his mother was buried under the debris even as the search operation is underway at Payyanithottam in Poonjar.

Even though Joseph was rescued, he succumbed to injuries while being shifted to the hospital.

Landslides and flooding across Kerala

Several parts of the Idukki district have reported landslides and flooding. At Upputhara, a parked police jeep was damaged in a landslide.

With the Pullakayar river overflowing, the Kokkayar low-level crossing (chappath) has been submerged. Around six houses were inundated in the surrounding area, and the affected families were shifted to safer locations, officials said.

Authorities said many other landslides have been reported from different parts of the district.

Heavy rain also disrupted traffic at multiple locations. The road between Kattappana and Vazhavara was blocked following a landslide, while rising water levels in the Chottupara stream at Vandiperiyar led to waterlogging on National Highway 183. The road at Nellimala was also blocked, affecting vehicular movement.

In the neighbouring Kottayam district, heavy rain triggered widespread flooding in Erattupetta, Kanjirappally, Koottickal and Erumeli, inundating residential areas, disrupting traffic and prompting large-scale rescue operations.

.Heavy rainfall continues to lash Kodagu; all schools shut .

Erattupetta town saw a sudden rise in water levels overnight, forcing authorities to halt vehicular traffic. Several houses, including those in Nadakkal and Murikkoly, were flooded.

Meanwhile, rescue teams, assisted by locals, evacuated people stranded on the upper floors of their homes to safer locations. Traffic in the area remained completely disrupted, according to officials.

In Koottickal and Mundakkayam, water levels continued to rise after the Manimala and Pullakayar rivers overflowed. The Koottickal causeway and low-level crossing were submerged, while water entered several houses.

Traffic was also affected after the Mundakkayam causeway went underwater.

Further, landslides were reported from the hilly areas of Pathanamthitta district.

Ranni MLA Pazhakulam Madhu, in a social media post, said heavy flooding had been reported in Ranni and adjoining areas, while urging people to remain cautious as river water levels had risen to dangerous levels and said floodwaters had entered several houses and shops.

Several parts of Ranni and nearby areas are cut off due to the flood, and the district administration has deployed boats to rescue people trapped in their houses, officials said.

Authorities said heavy rain, accompanied by landslides, caused a sudden rise in the water level in the Pampa river.

Relief camps have also been set up in Pathanamthitta district, officials added.

Apart from central Kerala, heavy rain was reported in the hilly areas of Kollam district. Floods and minor landslides were reported in Kozhikode, Malappuram and Palakkad districts.

IMD red alert

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast continued heavy rainfall in parts of Kerala. Rescue teams are on high alert, while people in vulnerable areas have been advised to maintain caution.

The IMD issued a red alert predicting very heavy rain in Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Idukki, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.

An orange alert has been issued for Ernakulam, Thrissur and Palakkad districts.

District administrations announced holidays for educational institutions in several districts, considering the forecast of heavy rain on Saturday.

(With PTI inputs)

articles.full_text:
Ahmedabad Cover Story
City on Red Alert after heavy rain warning by IMD
Two days of intense rains likely across Gujarat; AMC cancels staff leave, rescue teams on standby
A satellite view of clouds hovering over Gujarat at 6 pm on Thursday
Ahmedabad has been placed under a Red Alert after the India Meteorological Department (IMD) warned of heavy to very heavy rain, with isolated extremely heavy spells, over the next two days. The weather office has cautioned that intense rainfall, accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and winds of 30-40 kmph, could trigger waterlogging and disrupt normal life across parts of the city.
The warning comes as a deep depression over central India moves westwards, strengthening monsoon activity across Gujarat.
While South Gujarat is expected to bear the brunt of the system, Ahmedabad has also been placed in the highest warning category for Friday and Saturday due to the likelihood of extremely heavy rainfall.
Along with Ahmedabad, Anand, Vadodara, Bharuch, Surat, Tapi, Dang, Navsari, Valsad, Bhavnagar and Botad are under Red Alert on Friday. Narmada district faces the highest risk, with the IMD forecasting isolated extremely to exceptionally heavy rainfall. On Saturday, Ahmedabad, Anand, Surendranagar and Rajkot will remain under Red Alert, while several other districts continue under Orange and Yellow alerts.
The IMD expects widespread rain across Gujarat until August 3 before activity gradually eases. Residents have been advised to avoid unnecessary travel during heavy spells and stay updated with official weather advisories.
In view of the Red Alert, the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) has cancelled the leave of all officers and employees with immediate effect. Civic staff currently on leave have been directed to report back by 9 pm on Thursday, and no fresh leave will be sanctioned until further orders.
The Ahmedabad Fire and Emergency Services has also intensified its preparedness. Divisional Fire Officer Swastik Jadeja told Mirror, “All fire personnel are on duty, and our best swimmers and rescue teams are ready. Boats, life jackets, ropes, chainsaws, portable pumps and other emergency equipment have been deployed so we can respond swiftly to flooding, tree falls and rescue calls.”
AMC Commissioner Banchhanidhi Pani has directed all department heads to ensure officials remain at their respective stations for a rapid response to any emergency.
Additional Chief Secretary (Revenue) Jayanti Ravi reviewed measures at the State Emergency Operation Centre and instructed district administrations to remain on maximum alert. Collectors of Surat, Vadodara, Ahmedabad, Bhavnagar, Bharuch, Anand, Narmada, Tapi, Dang, Chhota Udepur, Panchmahal, Dahod and Mahisagar joined the high-level video conference.
Mild quake felt in A’bad
A mild earthquake measuring 2.6 on the Richter scale shook Ahmedabad at 4.39 am on Thursday. According to the Institute of Seismological Research (ISR), Gandhinagar, the epicentre was located about 29 km south-southwest of the city at a depth of 20 km.

Check full weather forecast here as the state battles heavy rainfall. Gujarat continues to be on India Meteorological Department's (IMD) red alert, a day after heavy rains battered the state, resulting in waterlogging in several areas and disrupting daily life. In the wake of deep depression over southwest Madhya Pradesh, extremely heavy rainfall is likely today. articles.full_text:
Kerala Heavy Rain Alert: Check Your District's Alert Status
Here's where things stand as the rain bands sweep across the state:Under Orange Alert (heavy to very heavy rain, 11.5–20.4 cm expected): Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod.
Comparatively safer for now (yellow alert or lighter): Thrissur, Palakkad and Malappuram, though residents here shouldn't let their guard down, since the system feeding this rain is expected to stay active over the coming days.
An orange alert, for anyone unfamiliar with the colour code, isn't the most severe warning Kerala can get, that's red, reserved for extremely heavy rainfall and genuine emergencies. But orange is still serious business. It means authorities expect rain heavy enough to disrupt daily life, flood low-lying pockets and make travel risky, especially in hilly and coastal stretches.
Kerala Schools Closed in Four Districts
The disruption has already spilled into everyday routines. District collectors in Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Wayanad and Kasaragod have declared a holiday for educational institutions, and the same order applies to Thamarassery and Vadakara taluks in Kozhikode.It's not just regular schools that are shut. The holiday covers anganwadis, religious study classes, tuition centres, special coaching classes and even professional colleges. One exception, though, residential schools and residential colleges remain open, since their students aren't out commuting on flooded roads to begin with.
If you're in one of these districts, it's worth checking with your local collectorate for updates, since holiday orders in Kerala tend to get extended or revised through the day depending on how the rain behaves.
Kerala Weather Forecast: Why the Rain Won't Ease Up
Behind this stretch of bad weather is what meteorologists call an offshore trough, a long, stretched-out belt of low pressure running along the coast, from south Gujarat all the way down to north Kerala. It works like a channel, continuously funnelling moisture-heavy winds toward the coastline and feeding one rain band after another instead of letting the weather settle.IMD data indicates this system isn't weakening in a hurry. The northern districts, Kannur, Kasaragod, Kozhikode and Wayanad, are likely to keep bearing the worst of it over the next few days as the trough stays parked over the region.
Kerala Weather Update: State put on alert
Fishermen along the Kerala coast have been told to stay off the water until conditions improve, the sea is expected to stay rough with squally winds making it unsafe to venture out. Authorities are also flagging the usual monsoon dangers that come with this kind of rainfall: trees toppling onto power lines, waterlogging in low-lying colonies, and damage to weaker structures. People living in landslide-prone hill areas or close to riverbanks have been asked to stay alert and move to safer ground if local officials issue such advice.If your district is on that orange list, it's not a day to take chances. Keep tabs on the latest bulletins rather than assuming the worst has passed just because the rain lets up for an hour or two. Kerala's monsoon has a habit of coming back stronger right when you least expect it.

Temperatures have soared to over 40 degrees in Florence, Modena and Terni, with ‘super-tropical’ nights where the minimum temperature does not drop below 25 degrees. The fourth heatwave of the year – which began this week following those that hit the country in late May, the second half of June and mid-July – shows no sign of letting up in Italia, but the situation is set to worsen further. Over the weekend, according to forecasts by Lorenzo Tedici of iLMeteo.it, ‘temperatures of 41 degrees are expected in Terni and 40 degrees in Ferrara, Mantua, Modena and Parma, with these levels set to persist at least until Monday’.
Highest alert
The Ministry of Health’s daily bulletin on heatwaves shows an exponential rise in the number of cities on ‘red alert’ – the highest alert level – which indicates emergency conditions with potential adverse effects even on the health of healthy, active people, and not just the most vulnerable groups. Yesterday there were 11; today there are 19; and tomorrow that figure will rise to 23. Of the 27 urban centres being monitored, therefore, on Sunday 2 August, only Ancona, Bari, Messina (which will be on ‘orange’) and Reggio Calabria (on ‘yellow’) will not be on ‘red’.
According to the opposition, the government is not doing enough to mitigate the effects of climate change. In a video posted on her social media pages, PD leader Elly Schlein emphasised that ‘cities cannot be left to the inaction and inertia of a government that is underestimating just how real and, unfortunately, tangible the impact of the climate emergency is’.
According to Schlein, the heatwave currently affecting Italia “is not normal. And no, we must not get used to it, as those on the right are saying. We must prepare ourselves. There have already been 12,000 deaths in Europe due to this latest heatwave and, sadly, the climate emergency continues to claim lives in our country too. Think, above all, of the elderly who are afraid to leave their homes in this heat: this, too, is urban safety.”
Forest fires
The wildfire crisis is also intensifying. According to data released by ISPRA, the Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research, during the second ten-day period of July, the areas of Europe affected by wildfires increased significantly: the figure is around 225 square kilometres a day, as if an area roughly twice the size of Paris were burning every day.
